This kinds of issues are best figured out using a debugger and actually stepping through what is going on while stuff gets corrupted. So having any form of reproduction is very important to address this with a fix instead of a rollback.

As for an MRP. I'm not sure how you are approaching it, but you should try the reduction strategy instead of building something from scratch.

Basically start out with your full project (in a copy obviously!) and then gradually remove stuff and see if it's still reproducible after the removal.

Start with stuff that is probably unrelated to the issue and safe to remove. For this issue I'd say that would be assets, nodes in the scenes that have no script attached and probably scenes that are not involved with the issue -> regularly make sure along the way, that the issue still reproduces and maybe use git commits to save snapshots were the issue is still present, so that you can rollback when too much stuff was removed.

The result does not need to be perfectly minimal and I can reduce further myself if I have a starting point. So just try to get the project down to something that you are fine with sharing (e.g. removing all the assets) and that reproduces the issue consistently.

Stuff gets inconsistent at the same spot that I mentioned here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/98141#issuecomment-2647818265

Some internal script depends on the player script. After the export the internal script gets freed and during that process it removes the player script from the GDScript cache. However the player script is not freed and still exists (it's loaded and referenced by the script editor).

At some later point a new script object gets created and takes over the path, because the existing instance is not present in the GDScript cache anymore. The old instance gets converted to an unnamed script because another script object took over the path.

My PR probably introduced some new code that relies on consistent state. But the issue that corrupts the state was already present before. 

@adamscott you originally introduced this clearing behaviour. Could you explain what this is meant to do? As stated in the other comment, I can't really make sense of the code snippet.

Or more specific: Why does `get_must_clear_dependencies` decide that it needs to clear dependencies that clearly are still in use somewhere else?

> [@adamscott](https://github.com/adamscott) you originally introduced this clearing behaviour. Could you explain what this is meant to do? As stated in the other comment, I can't really make sense of the code snippet.
> 
> Or more specific: Why does `get_must_clear_dependencies` decide that it needs to clear dependencies that clearly are still in use somewhere else?

It relates to cyclic references, because it artificially increases the reference count. It was my solution to detect and prevent leaked "islands".

To cite myself in #67714
>Let's bring back our example, but with a cyclic reference. Let's say `Main` loads `A` that loads `B` that loads back `A`.
>
>Here, `Main` reference count is 1 (referenced by the engine), `A` is 2 (referenced by `Main` and `B`) and `B` is 1 (referenced by `A`).
>
>Do you see the issue? When `Main` will be deleted, there will be no way to delete `A` and `B`. `A` will lose its reference to `Main` and will decrement, but it will not be deleted as `A` reference count is now 1. `B` is not deleted because it didn't lose its reference to `A`.

Ideally, that should be replaced by @reduz's proposal/PR: #90576.
